sections.history: Tirthanagiri lies in the Nadu Nadu country, the belt of villages between the Kaveri delta and the northern Tamil plains, and is among the old Shaiva shrines named in the Tevaram, where the town is called Tiruthinainagar. Tradition counts it among the temples praised by the saint Sundarar, whose hymn is gathered in the seventh Tirumurai and names the place and the Lord in every verse, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The presiding Shiva is honoured as Sivakozhundeesar, read as the Lord who is the tender shoot, worshipped here as a self-manifested (swayambhu) linga. Raised and enlarged in stone by the medieval patrons of the Tamil country and kept in daily worship ever since, the temple has carried the memory of the hymn-singing age into the present.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a three-tiered rajagopuram, its gateway set in line with the flagstaff, the seated Nandi, and the balipeetam in the manner the tradition prescribes. Within, the sanctum holds the swayambhu linga of Sivakozhundeesar, while the goddess Oppila Nayaki is honoured in her own shrine. Around the sanctum the niches carry the customary attendant deities — Dakshinamurthi the silent teacher, Lingodbhava, and Durga — and the enclosure keeps the measured, unhurried plan of a village temple of the Nadu Nadu country. For a few days around the Panguni full moon the light of the sun is said to fall directly upon the linga, a solar alignment the temple keeps with pride.
sections.legends: The story most often told at Tirthanagiri is of a devoted farming couple of the village, remembered as Periyan and his wife, whose unbroken vow was never to take their own meal until they had first fed a servant of Shiva. Through a season of hardship they kept the vow without fail, and the Lord, it is said, came to prove and to bless their steadfastness, so that their small store never ran empty and their field yielded against all expectation. From this the temple carries the lesson that the Lord receives the food given in his devotees' name as though given to himself, and the tale is recalled with affection by those who come to pray here.
sections.festivals: As at every Shiva temple, Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are kept with care, and the Tamil month of Margazhi and the new-year month of Chithirai draw the fullest gatherings. The Panguni days when the sun's light is said to reach the sanctum are observed with special worship. Dates follow the Tamil calendar and shift each year, so confirm them locally before setting out.
sections.experience: Tirthanagiri rewards a quiet visit, away from the larger pilgrim routes. Enter beneath the eastern gopuram, come before the self-manifested linga of Sivakozhundeesar, and turn to the goddess Oppila Nayaki in her shrine. Many who come carry in mind the story of the couple who fed the Lord's devotees, and offer their prayers in that same spirit. The temple stands among the fields and small roads of the Cuddalore countryside, and keeps the calm of a very old village sanctuary.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tirthanagiri lies in the Cuddalore district, reached via Alappakkam, roughly 25 km from Chidambaram and about 27 km from Cuddalore town. Buses running between Cuddalore and Chidambaram serve the village; Chidambaram and Virudhachalam are the nearest railheads, and Puducherry and Tiruchirappalli the nearest airports. Confirm the final approach locally.
